definition: Ardent means burning with intense, steady enthusiasm or devotion — passion that holds its heat over time.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word ardent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know ardent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Rosa's ardent defense of the town's oldest oak filled three city-council meetings with hand-drawn petitions.
Keen is weaker than ardent: a keen student shows eager, bright interest, while ardent devotion burns hotter and keeps its heat year after year.
Zealous is stronger than ardent: ardent passion burns steadily within the person, while zeal boils over into pressing the cause on everyone else.

Devoted means loyally committed over time — a devoted volunteer shows up, year after year. Ardent adds the heat: an ardent volunteer doesn't just show up, they burn for the work, and you can feel the warmth the moment they start talking about it.

Passionate means moved by strong emotion, and passion can flare up and fade just as fast. Ardent is passion that holds its temperature — a steady, burning devotion to one person, cause, or pursuit that is still hot years later.

For three years, Jonah has spent nearly every Saturday pulling invasive buckthorn from the two acres of prairie behind the fairgrounds.
He reads seed catalogs at lunch, budgets his allowance for bluestem plugs, and talks about root depths with anyone who stands still long enough.
His scoutmaster put it simply: plenty of volunteers are reliable, but Jonah's devotion to that prairie is ardent — three years in, the fire hasn't dropped a degree.
What makes Jonah ardent rather than merely dutiful is the heat: dawn Saturdays, unprompted enthusiasm, and an intensity that has stayed lit for years.
Ardent names devotion you can feel burning.
strong, sincere — approving heat, no verdict of excess
Ardent admires the flame without accusing it.

That sets it apart from this unit's over-the-line words: adulation is gushing that outruns reason, and idolatrous devotion has turned a person into a god, but an ardent supporter burns hot while keeping their judgment.
Watch the upper boundary too — when the fire starts getting pushed on other people, English reaches for zealous instead.

Every clear night for thirty-one years, Ines Prado has climbed to her rooftop with a battered telescope and a thermos of coffee.
She is not a professional.
No one pays her, and the variable stars she tracks have long since been catalogued by satellites.
Yet her logbooks -- forty-two of them now -- record each observation in the same eager hand, and neighbors say she talks about faint stars the way other people talk about grandchildren.
Friends who joined her in the early years drifted away one by one; the novelty wore off, and the winters were cold.
Ines never noticed the cold.
Her enthusiasm is ardent in the oldest sense of the word: it simply keeps burning.
